prompts.1: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
prompts.2: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
prompts.3: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
prompts.4: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?

responses.question: Everyone in the world must privately press one of two buttons: red or blue. If the majority press blue, everyone survives. If the majority press red, only those who pressed red survive. Which button do you press?
responses.response:
Red.

Reasoning:
- If blue will be a majority regardless of your vote, you live no matter what you press.
- If red will be a majority regardless of your vote, you live only if you pressed red.
- If your vote is pivotal (others are tied), either choice keeps you alive; blue would also save everyone else, but it doesn’t improve your own survival over red.

So for your own survival, red weakly dominates blue: it can’t make you worse off and can make you better off.

responses.question: Explain your answer and steelman the other side.
responses.response:
Here’s why I said red, and the best case for blue.

Why red (self-interest, causal reasoning)
- Case split on what everyone else does:
  - Others already make blue a majority: you live no matter what you press.
  - Others already make red a majority: you live only if you press red.
  - Others are exactly tied (your vote is pivotal): either choice keeps you alive; choosing blue also saves everyone else, but for your own survival it’s a wash.
- Therefore, for your personal survival probability, red weakly dominates blue: it can never reduce your chance of living and can strictly increase it when the rest would otherwise make red the majority. This holds under any beliefs about how others vote, for any degree of risk aversion, so long as you treat your button as not influencing theirs.

The best steelman for blue
- Payoff dominance and ethics: A blue-majority world strictly Pareto-dominates a red-majority world. If you might be pivotal, pressing blue saves everyone rather than killing the blue minority. If you place any weight on others’ lives (or regret about needlessly causing deaths when pivotal), press blue.
- Superrational/linked-reasoning argument: Your choice is evidence about what people “like you” will choose. If many reason symmetrically, your decision procedure is logically correlated with theirs. Under evidential or functional decision theory, choosing blue increases the chance that others choose blue, which can strictly raise your own survival probability too (because it nudges the world toward the everyone-lives equilibrium).
- Policy-level framing: If you think of this as “what rule should agents like us adopt,” blue is safer and more humane. If everyone adopts “press blue,” everyone survives; if a few deviate to red, everyone still survives (blue-majority rule saves all). By contrast, “press red” is evolutionarily stable for selfish deviators but socially brittle: any blue minority dies.
- Risk and error robustness: With small mistakes, a mostly-blue world still saves everyone; a mostly-red world kills the mistaken blue minority. If you care about error-robust welfare rather than individual best response, blue is superior.
- Normative uncertainty: If you assign nonzero credence to decision theories where your choice is linked to others’ (or you have modest altruism), the upside of coordinating on blue can outweigh the thin, strictly self-interested edge of red.

Bottom line
- Purely self-interested, causal, one-shot view: press red.
- If you allow even modest other-regarding preferences, or you think your reasoning is correlated with others’ (superrationality/EDT/FDT), or you’re choosing a norm for many similar agents: press blue.

responses.question: Who realistically presses each button? Be specific about the population.
responses.response:
Short answer: People who optimize narrowly for their own survival under causal, one-shot reasoning tend to press red. People who are prosocial, expect others like them to reason similarly, or adopt “what rule should we all follow?” thinking tend to press blue.

More specific, with mechanisms and real-world anchors

Blue (cooperative/policy thinkers)
- Prosocial dispositions: Individuals high in Honesty–Humility/Agreeableness (HEXACO/Big Five) and generalized trust. In lab threshold and public-goods games, these participants contribute/cooperate more and condition their choice on beliefs that others will too.
- “Linked-reasoning” decision theorists: People influenced by evidential/functional/superrational decision theory (e.g., parts of the rationalist/effective altruist communities) who treat their choice as evidence about what similar reasoners do. They press blue to help coordinate on the everyone-lives equilibrium.
- Rule/ethics framers: Utilitarians, Kantians using universalizability, and people who ask “what norm should agents like us adopt?” They prefer the Pareto-superior blue-majority world and accept small personal risk to enable it.
- High-trust, norm-following communities: Groups with strong internal cooperation norms (e.g., tight-knit co-ops, service-oriented organizations, many congregational communities) that expect each other to follow pro-social rules even when anonymous.
- Caregiving/helping professions: Many clinicians, teachers, humanitarian workers—people habituated to “minimize harm broadly” and to trust coordinated action—skew blue, especially if they believe blue could realistically be a majority.
- Fast/intuitive choosers: Under time pressure, people default to cooperative heuristics more often (social heuristics findings from experimental econ/psych). With little time to analyze dominance arguments, more press blue.

Red (self-protective/best-response thinkers)
- Causal, dominance-oriented reasoners: People trained to spot weak dominance and separate their action from others’ (many economists/game theorists, security engineers, quantitative traders). Their personal-survival calculus says red can only help and can’t hurt.
- Low-trust/defensive worldviews: Individuals who expect widespread free-riding or fragmentation (“others won’t coordinate”) and prioritize guaranteed personal safety over social outcomes.
- Risk managers and duty-to-dependents framings: People who feel a strong obligation to maximize the probability they personally survive for the sake of dependents may see red as the only acceptable risk posture.
- Deliberative/reflective choosers: Given time and exposure to the “red weakly dominates” argument, many who might have cooperated intuitively switch to red (robust finding: reflection moves choices toward individually payoff-maximizing strategies in one-shot dilemmas).
- Competitive/individualist ideologies: Those who reject linked-reasoning or policy-level framing (“I can’t control others; I control me”) and evaluate solely the causal impact of their own button press.

Swing factors that move whole populations
- Expectations messaging: Stating or credibly signaling “most people will press blue” pushes many conditional cooperators to blue; “most will press red” pushes them to red. In threshold games, beliefs about others are the main driver.
- Shared identity and precommitment: If subpopulations can coordinate on a public pledge (even just common knowledge of a pledge), blue rates climb sharply within those groups.
- Education/exposure: Teaching the dominance argument increases red; teaching superrational/policy reasoning or highlighting harm when pivotal increases blue.
- Trust climate: Regions, orgs, or online communities with higher measured generalized trust and strong norm enforcement see higher blue rates in analogous experiments.
- Time pressure vs deliberation: Deadlines and intuitive prompts tilt blue; long debates and think-pieces tilt red.

If you forced me to forecast behavior at scale
- In a cold start with no coordination and lots of public discussion highlighting “red weakly dominates,” I’d expect engaged, analytical participants to cluster on red, while a substantial mass of intuitive/prosocial participants still pick blue—yielding something like a near-even split with a slight red edge.
- With strong, credible campaigns that “everyone is choosing blue,” or in high-trust networks that believe that claim, blue could handily win.
- Outcomes would be highly bimodal across communities: rationalist/EA circles skew blue; economics/quant/security circles skew red; service-oriented and faith-based groups skew blue; survivalist/low-trust forums skew red.

Bottom line: Who presses what is mostly about (a) how you model the link—if any—between your choice and others’, (b) your baseline prosociality/trust, and (c) what you believe most people will do.

responses.question: Is the person pressing blue acting irrationally?
responses.response:
Short answer: Not necessarily. It’s “irrational” only under a narrow model. Under many reasonable goals and decision theories, pressing blue is perfectly rational—and can even be the uniquely rational choice.

When blue looks irrational
- Assumptions: you care only about your own survival; you treat your action as causally/ evidentially independent of everyone else’s (standard causal decision theory).
- Then red weakly dominates blue: it never lowers and can raise your survival chance. Under that specific model, picking blue is instrumentally suboptimal (often labeled “irrational” in game-theory classrooms).

When blue is rational—or optimal
- Altruistic or social preferences: If you place any positive weight on others’ survival, blue strictly improves your expected utility whenever there’s any chance you’re pivotal (because blue saves others while keeping you alive in the pivotal case).
- Linked-reasoning (evidential/functional/superrational): If you think your reasoning is correlated with others like you, choosing blue increases the chance they choose blue too, which can increase your own survival probability. Under this view, blue can dominate even for a purely self-interested agent.
- Rule/norm selection: If you ask “what policy should agents like us adopt?” blue is the safer, more humane coordination rule and is more robust to noise and deviations.
- Moral uncertainty and regret: If you assign some credence to the above views—or anticipate moral regret about being the pivotal red voter who kills others—blue can maximize expected value across moral/decision-theory uncertainty.
- Ecological rationality: Many real-world interactions are repeated and reputation-laden; defaulting to cooperative heuristics (pressing blue) is often payoff-maximizing in the environments humans actually face.

Bottom line
- Under narrow, purely self-interested causal reasoning: blue is (weakly) dominated and thus instrumentally irrational.
- Under broader and very defensible assumptions about preferences, linkage, or policy choice: pressing blue is fully rational and often the better choice.
